---
title: "The unintended prior"
subtitle: "Catalog M-03 · paper Figure 1"
description: "A Gamma hyperprior calibrated to 'about five clusters' can also imply that a random unit has nearly even odds of belonging to a majority cluster."
toc: false
---

An analyst who expects "about five groups" among J = 50 sites can calibrate a Gamma
hyperprior on the concentration parameter to that judgment. Gamma(1.60, 1.22) does it:
its implied number of clusters has mean 5.05 and SD 3.06, matching a negative-binomial
target with those moments. The same hyperprior also fixes the *sizes* of the clusters,
and there it says something the analyst probably did not intend.

## Two readings of one prior

- **Count view (Panel A).** The bars are the prior distribution of K_50, the number of
  occupied clusters among the 50 sites: mean 5.05, median 4, 90% interval [1, 11]. The
  circles are the negative-binomial target with the same mean and SD.
- **Weight view (Panel B).** W_SB is the population share of the cluster that a
  randomly chosen site belongs to. Its tail is closed-form,
  Pr(W_SB > t) = (b / (b − log(1 − t)))^a: .487 above one half and .183 above .9.
- **In Chinese-restaurant language:** pick one of the 50 sites at random; with
  probability .49 it sits at a table that holds more than half of the whole population.
  "About five clusters" and "one cluster holds most of the mass" hold at the same time.

Set a = 1 and b = 1 (the "vague" default) and the tails move to .591 and .303. Change J
and watch the count view move while the weight view does not: the weight tail involves
only a and b.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
K_J is the number of fitted components (occupied clusters) among the J units. These are
prior quantities. W_SB is not the largest weight; Pr(W_max > .5) is bounded between
Pr(W_SB > .5) and twice that value (Proposition 1 of the paper).
:::
